# A Matter of Trust

Robert sits across from me with his hands folded carefully in his lap, a habit born from forty-seven years in sales—the kind of composed posture that puts clients at ease. At seventy, he still wears his blazers well, still maintains the practiced smile that once came naturally. Now, though, I notice how his jaw tightens when the office door closes behind us.

Three years ago, Robert was leaving a client dinner in downtown Milwaukee. He'd just closed a significant deal for commercial real estate—the kind of success that had defined his career. Walking to his car around nine in the evening, he was approached by two men in the parking garage. They wanted his wallet. Robert, accustomed to negotiating, tried to reason with them. He remembers thinking he could talk his way out of it, the same way he'd talked his way into countless contracts.

One of the men had a knife.

When Robert didn't hand over his wallet fast enough, the blade caught him across the ribs. The physical wound healed within weeks—a surgical repair, some scarring. The other wound has proven more persistent.

He stopped going to client dinners after that. His sales numbers, which had been climbing steadily toward retirement, began to slip. Robert's wife, Margaret, initially attributed it to age, but she knew better. She watched him check the locks three times before bed. She noticed he no longer wanted to drive downtown, no longer wanted to go anywhere after dark. The man who had spent decades building relationships with clients now found himself avoiding the very situations that had made him successful.

When Robert does venture out during daylight hours, he's hypervigilant in ways that exhaust him. In parking garages—which he must sometimes visit for work—his heart rate spikes before he even reaches his car. He scans for exits, for other people, for anything that might be a threat. A raised voice from another customer makes him flinch. He's developed a habit of sitting with his back to the wall in restaurants, something Margaret gently teases him about, though she understands why.

The intrusive thoughts come without warning. He'll be reviewing a contract and suddenly he's back in that garage, feeling the shock of the blade, the hot sting of blood. His hands shake for twenty minutes afterward. Sleep has become unreliable—he wakes at 3 a.m. most nights, his heart pounding from dreams he can't quite remember but can certainly feel.

What troubles Robert most is the erosion of something fundamental. He's always been a man who trusted people, who believed in the basic goodness of strangers. That trust feels like a luxury he can no longer afford. When young salespeople on his team talk about networking events or evening client meetings, Robert hears danger in their plans. He finds himself warning them, offering to take over their evening commitments, unable to articulate why without sounding paranoid.

Margaret has been patient, but Robert senses the strain. She wants her husband back—the one who walked into rooms with confidence, who believed the best of people, who wasn't afraid of the dark. He wants that man back too. But when he closes his eyes, he's still in that garage, and the world still feels like a place where violence can find you when you least expect it, where your ability to negotiate and persuade means nothing against someone with a knife and nothing to lose.
